An open-source multi-sensor eddy current database for non-destructive characterisation of carbon fibre structures and analysis framework for eddy current inspection of CFRP composites
abstract: Open, standardised non-destructive testing (NDT) datasets for carbon fibrereinforced polymers (CFRP) are scarce, which hinders reproducibility,algorithm benchmarking, and data-driven defect characterisation in thecomposites community. This paper introduces EddyCus-HDF5, a publiclyavailable database comprising 738 eddy current scan files acquired with eightsensors (three absolute, five half-transmission) manufactured by Fraunhofer IKTS,covering five or more CFRP material systems and eight defect categories ateigen frequencies between 4\,MHz and 24.3\,MHz. The accompanyingopen-source Python software pipeline converts proprietary EddyCusASCII exports into a structured HDF5 format with full specimen, sensor, andinstrument metadata, and simultaneously indexes all scans into a queryableSQLite database. Two integrated signal-processing methods are presented:(i)~phase rotation for contrast optimisation, which scans the complex rotationangle $\theta \in [0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ and selects the angle maximising auser-defined standard-deviation contrast metric; and (ii)~Fourier-based fibreorientation detection (FOD), which extracts dominant yarn angles from the2D spatial frequency spectrum of each scan using a polar power analysis withbilinear interpolation. The dataset,converter software (MIT licence, v1.1.0), and example analysis notebooks areopenly available at https://github.com/itm-tud/eddycus-hdf5-converterand is archived on Zenodo with a persistent DOI. This resource providesthe NDT and composites research community with a reproducible foundation formachine learning and model benchmarking, sensor comparison, and algorithm development.

title: Enhanced carbon composites via graphite exfoliated on paper for high-performance flexible radar-absorbing materials
abstract: A novel strategy is proposed using pencil-exfoliated graphite on a paper substrate as a controllable resistive layer for a flexible Salisbury radar-absorbing material (RAM) architecture, governed by the modeling framework introduced. This approach leverages a natural, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly carbon source, avoiding toxic materials such as indium tin oxide (ITO) which is conventionally used for resistive layers. The method is simple, low-cost, and highly reproducible: conductive layers are created by drawing with standard graphite pencils on conventional paper, forming resistive sheets that can be integrated into Salisbury screen-type multilayer composites. By integrating graphite-on-paper layers with graphite-loaded silicone composite slabs on metallic substrates, the system achieves strong microwave reflectivity attenuation (–30 dB) across the C, X, and Ku bands, with a wide –10 dB bandwidth (BW) covering up to 83 % of the X-band. A theoretical model quantifies the effects of surface conductivity and dielectric permittivity, enabling precise tuning of both the absorption amplitude and frequency position. This allows the imaginary part of the permittivity to control attenuation intensity, while the real part determines the resonance frequency. The design offers flexibility, low environmental impact, and precise control of RAM performance.

title: Hydrophobic CNF/MXene composite aerogels with synergistic structure–interface engineering for reliable flexible sensing
abstract: Flexible piezoresistive aerogels are promising for wearable electronics and sensing in complex environments, yet their practical application is often limited by structural collapse during compression and moisture-induced conductive instability. Herein, an ultralight hydrophobic CNF/MXene composite aerogel is developed through synergistic structure–interface engineering. Directional freeze-casting creates vertically aligned lamellar channels that effectively confine compressive deformation and guide the assembly of MXene into continuous conductive pathways. Meanwhile, in situ vapor-phase deposition of methyltrichlorosilane (MTS) establishes a stable hydrophobic interface that suppresses moisture-induced softening and conductive fluctuations. Benefiting from the synergy between ordered structural regulation and interfacial stabilization, the resulting aerogel exhibits an ultralow density of 1.7 mg cm −3 , a water contact angle of 146.1°, and a high sensitivity of 438.65 kPa −1 over 0-98 kPa, together with stable operation over 1000 compression cycles. Reliable sensing performance is maintained under coupled high-temperature, high-humidity, and dynamic compression conditions. In addition, the aerogel demonstrates rapid photothermal conversion capability, reaching 179.6°C under light irradiation. This work provides a practical strategy for constructing environmentally reliable porous conductive aerogels and offers new insights into the cooperative regulation of deformation behavior and interfacial stability for flexible sensing applications.

title: Tentacle-like molecular architecture for superior low-temperature resistant performance in bio-based myrcene elastomer nanocomposites
abstract: Driven by the urgent demand for sustainable elastomers with excellent low-temperature resistant performance for winter tire applications, a novel bio-based elastomer was developed via a green synthetic strategy. A series of poly(myrcene-co-butadiene) (PMyBd) with tunable bio-based content were synthesized using bio-based myrcene and petroleum-based butadiene as comonomers through low-temperature redox emulsion polymerization. The incorporation of myrcene introduces bulky branched side groups that generate a tentacle-like molecular architecture along the backbone of PMyBd. This sterically extended architecture disrupts chain regularity, suppresses low-temperature crystallization, and maintains a low glass transition temperature (-77°C to -67 °C), resulting in outstanding low-temperature resistant performance. Reactivity ratio analysis indicates that the copolymerization follows a non-ideal azeotropic mechanism (azeotropic point is 0.395), favoring the formation of high-molecular-weight, nearly random copolymers. Upon silica reinforcement, the PMyBd/silica nanocomposites achieve tensile strengths of 11.4-15.6 MPa and simultaneously exhibit low rolling resistance, excellent cold resistance, and outstanding ice-skid resistance. Notably, the bulky side chains derived from myrcene enhance chain mobility and provide steric hindrance that suppresses filler re-aggregation, thereby facilitating a more homogeneous silica dispersion. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirm that the high fractional free volume of the PMyBd/silica nanocomposites constitutes a key structural basis for their superior low-temperature performance. This work presents a framework that integrates molecular design, interfacial regulation, and engineering performance optimization, offering a viable pathway toward sustainable high-performance elastomers for low-temperature applications.

Tailoring competitive reactivity of cyclotriphosphazene derivatives and their associated crosslinked condensed-state structure for high-modulus and interfacially robust T800 carbon fiber/bismaleimide composites
abstract: Fiber-reinforced bismaleimide composites is an important class of materials in advanced composites field. This work proposes a novel strategy to simultaneously improve the toughness and heat resistance of bismaleimide resin, as well as the interfacial property and flexural modulus of its composites by using butadiene-functionalized cyclotriphosphazene derivatives (BCPDs) to regulate the condensed state structure of the crosslinking network of bismaleimide resin. Guarded by the density functional theory (DFT) calculations, a series of BCPDs characterized by uniform substitution of alkane chains and butadiene groups onto cyclotriphosphazenes are synthesized. By tuning the alkyl chain length, the Diels-Alder reactivity between BCPDs and the cross-linking monomers can be precisely modulated, which in turn governs the topological structure of the cross-linked network and the resulting phase morphology. It is demonstrated that compared with the neat resin, the BD/T‑LB‑CP resin exhibits 77% higher char residue, 197% greater impact strength, and its carbon‑fiber composites show roughly 34% and 44% improvements in interlaminar shear strength and flexural strength, respectively. Furthermore, by modifying the reactive functional groups, this strategy can be extended to other thermosetting resin systems, demonstrating good versatility and application potential.

abstract: Sustainable, flexible, tough, and thermally conductive substrates are critically required for next-generation green electronics. While cellulose nanopaper has emerged as a promising platform due to its high mechanical strength, it still exhibits limited elongation and thermal conductivity. Herein, multiscale hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) was incorporated into a cellulose nanofiber (CNF) matrix to achieve a balanced combination of mechanical and thermal properties. Based on experimental results and Representative Volume Element (RVE) simulations, nanoscale h-BN enhances strength and flexibility by alleviating stress concentrations within the CNF matrix, whereas microscale h-BN forms continuous thermal conduction pathways to enable efficient heat transport. Compared with pristine CNF, the CNF/multiscale h-BN nanopaper exhibits a 52% increase in tensile strength, a 49% reduction in flexural stress, an 87% decrease in minimum bending radius, and a 100% enhancement in thermal conductivity. Moreover, the CNF/multiscale h-BN nanopaper exhibits mechanical strength and flexibility comparable to PI and PET, while achieving thermal conductivity approximately 10 times higher than that of PET and 5 times higher than that of PI. Electrical printing and heat dissipation demonstrations further validate its applicability as a sustainable substrate for next-generation flexible electronics.

title: Impact and damage tolerance of hybrid-core sandwich composites reinforced with Kevlar® wastes
abstract: This study presents the impact and compression after impact (CAI) strength of sandwich composites made from waste Kevlar® fibers and honeycomb papers. Polyurethane core was reinforced with waste short Kevlar® fibers in various ratios (2-10%), while the face composite was made Kevlar® from woven edge wastes. The core also contained recycled honeycomb paper with unit-cell widths of 10 and 20 mm. Waste Kevlar® yarns were also used in a robotic stitching machine for through-the-thickness reinforcement, simulating the hand stitching. Impact tests (50J-200J) revealed that the short fiber ratio, honeycomb paper unit-cell width, and through-the-thickness reinforcement have a significant effect on energy absorption and failure mechanism of sandwiches. As the short fiber ratio rises, more energy was absorbed, and as honeycomb paper unit-cell width increased, core compaction slowed down, resulting in more progressive crushing. However, the stitching process created pre-damage in the sandwich composites, negatively affecting impact resistance. It was observed that the CAI retention decreased with fiber reinforcement in the core, and the sample with the highest damage tolerance was the foam structure without fiber. The waste materials used (fiber, woven fabric edge, and honeycomb paper) did not hinder sandwich construction and highlight the potential of recycled composites.

title: Enhanced mechanical performance of resistance-welded thermoplastic composite joints via tailored laminate stacking and heating element alignment
An energy-consistent framework for shear correction in corrugated sandwich plates with soft cores
abstract: Accurate evaluation of the transverse shear correction factor is essential for reliable modelling of sandwich plates with soft cores, particularly when first-order shear deformation theories are employed. Classical shear correction factors, usually derived for homogeneous or weakly heterogeneous plates, may become inadequate for corrugated sandwich structures with pronounced stiffness contrast, where the soft core tightly fills the profiled space between corrugated facings. This study addresses the question of how an energy-consistent shear correction factor can be identified for such cross-sections without resorting to a full three-dimensional finite element model. A unified framework is proposed, combining a closed-form layered formulation with a pixel-based formulation of the cross-section. The layered solution provides a transparent analytical baseline for flat or homogenizable sandwich configurations, whereas the pixel-based formulation enables direct treatment of corrugated geometries in which the soft core fully occupies the profiled space formed by the corrugated facings. The method is based on strain-energy equivalence and evaluates the transverse shear stiffness from the spatial distribution of geometry and material properties. The results show that the identified shear correction factor is strongly affected by the reference shear modulus, material contrast, and core-dominated shear-energy localization. The obtained values therefore should be interpreted as energy-consistent stiffness scaling factors rather than universal constants. The proposed framework is computationally lightweight and can be directly incorporated into Mindlin–Reissner plate and shell models. Its scope is global stiffness correction; detailed local stress fields, thickness-stretching effects, and full three-dimensional validation remain subjects for future work.

Thermomechanical post-processing as a route to improved blast-like and puncture impact performance in 3D-printed Onyx/Kevlar laminates
abstract: Limited research has examined the impact response of printed continuous fibre reinforced polymer composites (CFRPCs) under blast-like and puncture loading, particularly when post-processing is applied. This study examines 3D-printed Kevlar CFRPCs manufactured with a 0°/90° fibre layup and nylon-based chopped carbon fibre matrix. Samples were subjected to thermomechanical post-processing under temperature–pressure combinations of 150–200 °C and 250–1000 kPa, followed by quenching. Performance was evaluated using complementary tests: air shock wave loading in a closed-end shock tube configuration with high-speed imaging and pressure measurements to quantify transient deflection; quasistatic four-point bending to measure flexural strength and modulus; and low velocity impact to quantify peak force and puncture energy. Post-processing temperature governs the response more strongly than pressure. Relative to as-printed CFRPC, treatment at 200 °C reduced shock-induced deflection by up to 69.2%, eliminated edge delamination in shock tube tests, and increased flexural strength by 34.0% and stiffness by 50.7%. Under puncture impact, the 200 °C condition exhibited a more progressive, extended load-bearing response, an +86.6% increase in puncture energy compared to as-printed samples, and a similar performance to a wet lay-up Kevlar/epoxy laminate. The improvements are associated with reduced interbead porosity, enhanced fibre wetting and suppressed interfacial delamination observed using microscopy and with thermally-induced nylon polymorphic evolution from a mixed γ / α structure to the complete α phase revealed using X-ray diffraction. Thermomechanical post-processing near the melting regime can shift printed Kevlar CFRPCs from interface-limited failure towards a more damage-tolerant response under blast-like and point-impact loading.

Correlating scale-specific void architecture with tensile and flexural performance in fused filament fabricated continuous carbon fibre-reinforced PA6-based composites
abstract: Continuous carbon fibre–reinforced thermoplastic composites produced by fused filament fabrication (FFF) exhibit mechanical properties influenced by manufacturing-induced voids near bead-fusion zones and fibre–matrix interfaces. In this work, a replicated 3 × 3 full-factorial design of experiments (DOE) quantified tensile strength (TS) and flexural strength (FS) across fibre volume content (20–40 vol%) and stacking sequence (Equidistant, Borders, and Borders & Centre) in continuous carbon fibre–reinforced Onyx composites (CFROC). A mechanically informed sub-DOE was then analysed using synchrotron micro-computed tomography (SMCT; 3.6 μm voxel edge length) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of as-printed surfaces. Connected void objects were segmented from SMCT volumes and partitioned by equivalent spherical diameter (ESD) into micro (ESD < 0.100 mm), meso (0.100 ≤ ESD < 0.500 mm), and macro (ESD ≥ 0.500 mm), with a flagged macro-tail subset (ESD ≥ 1.0 mm) used to capture deposition-scale discontinuities. Across the DOE, responses spanned TS = 230–435 MPa and FS = 399–636 MPa; the highest fitted responses occurred at 40 vol% with Borders, whereas 20 vol% with Equidistant defined the lower bound. In the SMCT subset, global porosity (Pglobal) ranged from 5.58 to 10.21%, but strength ranking was not explained by porosity magnitude alone. Ranking was more consistent with scale-resolved porosity partitioning, meso/macro discontinuity morphology, and macro-tail continuity. PO references showed connected macro discontinuity networks, whereas high-performing CFROC specimens exhibited curtailed macro-span continuity and a greater share of void volume in micro/meso populations; SEM observations supported corresponding differences in fusion quality and interface-adjacent discontinuities. The study presents a DOE-linked, object-wise, scale-resolved void-architecture framework for FFF CFROC that enables identification of mechanically consequential discontinuity families beyond Pglobal within a controlled reinforcement-architecture window.

title: Characterisation of the inter-ply sliding of biaxial non-crimp fabrics during the double diaphragm forming process
abstract: An experimental method for quantifying inter-fabric sliding in the double diaphragm forming (DDF) process is introduced. The approach employs grease markers with a standardised application and tracking procedure, ensuring consistency. An overlap experiment confirmed that the addition of markers had minimal influence on inter-fabric friction, enabling calibration between the marker elongation length and the actual sliding distance. The method reliably captured sliding when displacements exceeded 3~mm in the DDF experiments with different tool geometries. Comparisons with simulations showed agreement in sliding directions, although the magnitudes were numerically underestimated. The discrepancies highlight both experimental and modelling limitations. The proposed method offers a robust tool for investigating the direction of inter-fabric motion, advancing the study of inter-ply friction and guiding the optimisation of forming simulations.

abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP)/AL hybrid configurations have been widely utilized in aerospace and defense applications; however, their behavior and damage mechanisms under hypervelocity impact remain insufficiently understood. This paper presents an integrated experimental and numerical investigation of the hypervelocity impact response of composite plates comprising a CFRP layer and an aluminum backing plate. Six impact tests were conducted at velocities ranging from 2000 to 4000 m/s, encompassing both normal and oblique impact scenarios. High-speed photography was employed to capture the dynamic impact events, whereas post-impact computed tomography (CT) scanning enabled quantitative assessment of damage morphology. Numerical simulations were performed using the FEM-SPH adaptive coupling method to model the impact response. The damage mechanism of the composite plate was elucidated to occur in three stages: CFRP perforation, aluminum penetration, and debris expansion. CT scan analyses facilitated quantitative characterization of petaling damage in the aluminum backing plate, and the underlying formation mechanisms were elucidated through the sequential process of perforation, crack initiation, and crack propagation. Furthermore, a theoretical model describing petal curling was validated against CT-scan-based experimental measurements, demonstrating strong correlation. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the hypervelocity impact damage mechanisms in CFRP/AL composite plates and provides valuable insights into the design of composite protective structures.

abstract: This study investigated the thermo-oxidative aging of Poly(dimethylsiloxane-co-diphenylsiloxane) composite coatings reinforced with nano-fumed silica fillers at various temperatures, using heterogeneity as a key indicator of the aging process. Modulus profiling derived from nanoindentation tests were modeled with an exponential function to quantify these aging characteristics. Building on the principle of representing the cumulative state of aging, a growth model that accounts for the non-uniform nature of oxidation was developed by correlating "O2 consumption, degree of heterogeneity, modulus profiling, and parameter δ." Through mathematical expressions linking the relevant mechanical test parameters, a generalized kinetic equation connecting reaction mechanisms to real-world conditions was established, offering predictive capability for the performance of protective coatings.

title: Enhanced thermal conductivity of polyurethane composites via microstructural design of 3D interconnected boron nitride networks
abstract: To address the limitations of traditional thermal management materials, such as inefficient heat dissipation, thermal expansion mismatch, and inferior mechanical robustness, this study develops a three-dimensional (3D) continuous boron nitride aerogel (BNA)/polyurethane (PU) composite via microstructural design and interfacial engineering. Highly porous BNA is synthesized through a precursor polymerization and freeze-drying strategy, followed by surface hydroxylation to enhance interfacial compatibility. The resulting hydroxyl-functionalized BNA is infiltrated with an optimized PU matrix to construct a 3D continuous thermal network. Structural characterization confirms that the composite preserves the interconnected porous architecture of BNA, with PU uniformly filling the voids. Crucially, the hydroxyl-mediated interfacial interactions significantly reduce phonon scattering and thermal contact resistance. The optimized BNA-OH/PU composite achieves a thermal conductivity of 3.35 W/(m·K), exhibits thermal stability up to 310°C, and retains 94% of its mass after aging at 150°C for 10 days. Furthermore, the material demonstrates superior compression resilience and underwater adhesion, maintaining intact thermal pathways under cyclic loading. Thermal simulations and practical demonstrations in chip cooling and underwater electronics reveal performance considerably surpassing that of conventional thermal pads. This work provides a robust strategy for advancing polymer-based thermal composites, with significant potential for applications in electronics, aerospace, and extreme environments.

abstract: The development of useful micropatterning techniques for conductive polymer composites (CPCs) is crucial for stretchable device applications, yet remains challenging. We present a highly efficient and universal direct-writing strategy based on a facile mechanical scratch micropatterning (MSM) process for CPCs. Conductive composite sheets with designed functional micropatterns are prepared by controllably scratching a silver nanowire (AgNW) film with a mechanical tip, and transferring the patterned AgNW film onto a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix. The proposed MSM process not only enables a minimum strip width of 50 µm but also allows the facile creation of arbitrary AgNW/PDMS composite patterns according to the designed layout in a precise and highly reproducible manner. The MSM-processed interdigitated capacitive (MSMIC) composite electrodes are successfully utilized to demonstrate stretchable strain and touch sensors. Upon stretching up to 50%, the MSMIC sensor exhibits a high gauge factor (~0.43) with excellent linearity (R² ≈ 0.99) and negligible hysteresis. Further, it demonstrates a fast (~182 ms) and durable response (2000 cycles at 30% strain), and enables real-time human motion monitoring when worn. Moreover, the MSMIC sensor reliably responds to touch and is successfully scaled up to a 3 × 3 multipixel device for acquiring spatial tactile information.

Probabilistic predictions of process-induced deformation in carbon/epoxy composites using a Deep Operator Network
abstract: Fiber reinforcement and polymer matrix respond differently to manufacturing conditions due to mismatch in coefficient of thermal expansion and matrix shrinkage during curing of thermosets. These heterogeneities generate residual stresses over multiple length scales, whose partial release leads to process-induced deformation (PID), requiring accurate prediction and mitigation via optimized non-isothermal cure cycles. This study considers a unidirectional AS4 carbon fiber/amine bi-functional epoxy prepreg and models PID using a two-mechanism framework that accounts for thermal expansion/shrinkage and cure shrinkage. The model is validated against manufacturing trials to identify initial and boundary conditions, then used to generate PID responses for a diverse set of non-isothermal cure cycles (time-temperature profiles). Building on this physics-based foundation, we develop a data-driven surrogate based on Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets). A DeepONet is trained on a dataset combining high-fidelity simulations with targeted experimental measurements of PID. We extend this to a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) DeepONet, where branch-network features are modulated by external parameters, including the initial degree of cure, enabling prediction of time histories of degree of cure, viscosity, and deformation. Because experimental data are available only at limited time instances (for example, final deformation), we use transfer learning: simulation-trained trunk and branch networks are fixed and only the final layer is updated using measured final deformation. Finally, we augment the framework with Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI) to quantify uncertainty under experimental conditions and to support optimization of cure schedules for reduced PID in composites.

abstract: This study experimentally investigates the effects of prolonged radiation exposure on mechanical properties of high-strength, highly crystalline polyethylene (PE)/thermally reduced graphene oxide (TrGO) nanocomposite films for space applications. Prior to irradiation, PE/TrGO films were found to have tensile strengths up to ~4 GPa, more than 40 times that of conventional space-deployed membrane films (e.g., those used in solar sails) and over 59× the specific tensile strength. The PE/TrGO films were subjected to three radiation conditions to simulate space environmental conditions: 90Sr beta radiation (0.2 to 2.5 MeV), 80 keV electron beam irradiation, and 4.9 eV ultraviolet (254 nm) exposure. Under exposure to similar total ionizing doses (TID ~2.5 kGy, corresponding to ~3% of the unshielded annual electron dose in GEO) in a vacuum environment, the tensile strength showed little change after high-energy Sr-90 beta irradiation, but decreased by up to ~34.8% following intermediate-energy electron irradiation. Mechanical and Raman spectroscopic analyses were conducted to elucidate the radiation-induced structural and chemical changes before and after exposure, as well as to assess the protective effects of incorporated antioxidants on the stability of the PE films.

abstract: Pultruded planks are extensively utilized in critical load-bearing applications in the form of Pultruded Plank Laminated Structure (PLS), such as spar caps of wind turbine blades, due to their superior mechanical properties. However, their inherent toughness remains a bottleneck restricting structural reliability. Inspired by the nacre, this study proposes a "sacrificial" interfacial toughening strategy and develops a novel bio-inspired Pultruded Plank-Fabric Laminated Structure (PFLS). Challenging the conventional pursuit of defect-free interfaces, this design embeds fiber tows to lure crack tips into complex array—a logic consistent with "luring the enemy into the depths"—thereby triggering crack-pinning effects and high-efficiency energy dissipation mechanisms. DCB tests demonstrate that the ±45° configuration yields the optimal toughening effect, achieving an increase of over 100% compared to the baseline group. SEM characterization confirms that these embedded fibers promote intense crack deflection and fiber bridging. Furthermore, the theoretical formula is proposed for the programmable prediction of fracture toughness. Moreover, precise numerical simulation of crack propagation was achieved by incorporating a bilinear softening law within the Cohesive Zone Model. This research provides a bionic strategy that can be integrated into industrial production, and establishes a reliable design paradigm for the programmatic prediction of the interface behavior in advanced composites.

3D-printed carbon from fiber-filled polymer precursor with modular mechanical properties and in-plane dimensional accuracy
abstract: Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) have enabled the scalable fabrication of complex carbon structures with improved in-plane dimensional accuracy and control over their mechanical strength from plastic precursors. A key strategy in these approaches involves incorporating rigid filaments and additives, such as fibers, into precursor filaments to achieve structural control and mechanical property enhancement. This study first investigates the role of glass fiber (GF) filler loading on the transformation of 3D-printed polypropylene (PP) structures into carbon upon steps of sulfonation-induced crosslinking and pyrolysis. Increasing GF content in the PP precursor was found to accelerate crosslinking kinetics, driven by earlier onset of crack-assisted diffusion during sulfonation. Additionally, GF inclusion significantly reduced in-plane dimensional shrinkage during pyrolysis, enabling the production of geometrically stable carbon structures. At high loadings, GFs can also serve as mechanical reinforcements, enhancing both the strength and stiffness of the resulting carbon materials. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived carbon structures produced from PP-GF filaments can be reinforced through repeated infiltration and carbonization with phenolic precursors, resulting in significantly enhanced mechanical properties while preserving the integrity of their complex macrostructures. These findings highlight the potential of fiber-filled systems for the on-demand manufacturing of high-performance, carbon composites with improved in-plane dimensional retention.

Interfacial self-debonding in a basalt-polyacrylamide hydrogel composite enabling significant shrinkage mitigation in cementitious systems
abstract: Designing hydrogel-based composites for internal curing in cementitious systems remains challenging due to the persistence of polymer phases as discrete particles, which leads to hydrogel-related pore formation and reduces mechanical properties. In this study, a basalt–polyacrylamide hydrogel composite (BCPA) was engineered by introducing micron-sized basalt particles as physical crosslinking centers to construct a polymer–particle interface susceptible to external environment. Upon exposure to the ion-rich cement pore solution, ionic interactions, particularly Ca²⁺ complexation and cation adsorption on basalt surfaces, weaken the original polymer-basalt association, triggering interfacial self-debonding and subsequent redistribution of polyacrylamide segments within the cement matrix. This interfacial evolution induces a transition of the polymer phase from a discrete particulate state to a dispersed segmental configuration, thereby fundamentally altering the structural response of the hydrogel composite after incorporation. As a consequence, the characteristic pore scale associated with polymer collapse is significantly reduced, and hydrogel-related macropores are effectively mitigated. The redistributed polymer segments retain internal curing functionality while enabling a refined pore structure that can be readily accommodated by hydration products. At a dosage of 1 wt.%, BCPA reduces 7-day autogenous shrinkage by approximately 75% and decreases cracking area by nearly one order of magnitude, while limiting compressive strength loss within 20%, compared with approximately 44% for chemically crosslinked polyacrylamide. These findings demonstrate that regulating interfacial interactions to control polymer state evolution provides a viable strategy for designing hydrogel composites that reconcile shrinkage mitigation with mechanical integrity in cementitious systems.

title: Influence of needle-punching parameters on the dynamic mechanical behavior of recycled non-woven carbon fiber reinforced thermoplastics with controlled anisotropy
abstract: The escalating demand for sustainable and recyclable composite materials has drawn attention toward non-woven carbon fiber reinforced thermoplastics (NW-CFRTP), especially those utilizing recycled carbon fiber (rCF). Prior work on rCF/polyamide-6 (PA6) NW-CFRTP with a different CF grade and processing method has reported tensile strength up to 700 MPa and flexural strength up to 850 MPa, indicating the potential of such materials for structural and automotive applications. For needle-punched NW-CFRTP however, impact resistance and damage tolerance under bending impact remain insufficiently understood, limiting adoption in safety-critical applications. This work investigates three-point bending impact behavior of rCF/PA6 NW-CFRTP with controlled anisotropy, focusing on needle-punching densities (0, 28, 50, 100 punches/cm²) across longitudinal, transverse, and cross-ply configurations at 1.5 m/s. Instrumented impact testing, high-speed imaging, X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) micro-CT, and microscopy captured damage initiation and evolution. Needle-punching enhances specific energy absorption via through-thickness fiber bridging and suppressed delamination, enabling progressive rather than brittle failure; appropriately punched specimens exhibit higher absorbed energy and damage tolerance than unpunched ones. By analyzing peak force, energy absorption, and failure morphology, this study identifies an optimal needle-punching density around 50 punches/cm² that balances impact toughness and in-plane properties; the P50_M (longitudinal 50 needle-punching density) configuration attains a peak impact stress of 831 MPa and a specific energy absorption (SEA) of 516 J/kg. Finite element analyses reproduced the experimental results, confirming the optimal density. The findings provide guidance for processing–structure–performance tailoring of NW-CFRTP in lightweight components for transportation and related fields.

title: Sustainable carbon fiber production: Pilot-scale manufacturing and life cycle assessment of lignin–PAN blends
abstract: This study investigates the production, mechanical performance, environmental impact, and cost of carbon fibers (CFs) derived from lignin/polyacrylonitrile (PAN) blend precursors, with particular emphasis on the effect of residence time during thermal conversion. Up to 35 wt% organosolv lignin was incorporated into PAN, and the resulting blends were processed by wet spinning, followed by continuous stabilization and carbonization on a pilot-scale CF production line. The mechanical properties of the resulting CFs were evaluated as functions of lignin content and residence time. Fibers containing 20-30 wt% lignin achieved tensile strengths of 1.83-2.22 GPa and tensile moduli of up to 243 GPa, exceeding the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) targets for automotive applications of 1.72 GPa tensile strength and 172 GPa tensile modulus. However, fibers containing 35 wt% lignin exhibited increased brittleness and filament fusion at residence times longer than 6 min, limiting their processability. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction confirmed the formation of turbostratic carbon structures, with ratios, spacings, and crystallite dimensions comparable to those reported for high-strength carbon fibers. A cradle-to-gate life-cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted using pilot-scale manufacturing data. Incorporation of lignin reduced the estimated production cost by approximately 25% and lowered selected environmental impacts by up to 26%. However, these benefits were partly offset by the high energy demand of precursor production and carbonization. Overall, this study demonstrates the technical feasibility of producing automotive-grade lignin/PAN carbon fibers at pilot scale and highlights the trade-offs among mechanical performance, processability, cost, and environmental impact in bio-based carbon fiber manufacturing.

Tailoring the in-plane shear behavior and formability of woven preforms via hybrid slit-tufted modification: Mechanisms and modeling
abstract: In-plane shear response governs the formability of woven reinforcements during composite preforming, and its modification is central to defect mitigation in double-curved geometries. This study investigates the coupled effects of controlled slitting and tufting on the shear behavior of plain-woven E-glass fabric through picture frame tests combined with full-field optical measurements. Two slit configurations are examined: a diagonal slit (DS) aligned with the principal shear path, and a corner slit (CS) oriented along the warp/weft directions. Slitting is shown to act as a load-path reconfiguration mechanism rather than a simple stiffness reduction: DS creates a spatially extensive preferential release zone, while CS produces a more confined redistribution. Tufting introduces a deformation-dependent bridging constraint that remains passive at low shear angles and becomes progressively active beyond approximately 35°, partially suppressing slit-edge opening without significantly altering the broader shear angle field. Across all five specimen configurations, the shear locking angle remains invariant at approximately 44.0°, confirming that this geometric limit is governed by the intrinsic yarn packing condition and is insensitive to mesoscale structural modification. To quantify these coupled effects, a spatially weighted slit-opening ratio and a shear enhancement factor are introduced. A semi-empirical framework is developed for the DS configuration and reproduces the measured shear-force evolution with in the pre-locking regime. The CS configuration is excluded from the model because its slit-edge opening is negligible and the tufted and non-tufted responses are nearly indistinguishable. The framework encodes the locking angle invariance as a constitutive constraint, linking the modeling results directly to the experimental finding. These results provide a quantitative basis for mechanism-guided preform design targeting high-curvature composite structures.

title: Crack-connectivity-related damage evolution in 3D-printed fiber-reinforced recycled cementitious composites revealed by in-situ 4D CT
Strength enhancement of laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beams using steel bars
abstract: : This paper presents a novel method for reinforcing laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beams with steel bars, featuring a systematic comparison of four distinct reinforcing configurations. Experimental tests were conducted on full-scale beams with nominal dimensions of 45×160×3300 mm. The reinforcement consisted of 12 mm diameter B500SP steel bars bonded into pre-drilled grooves within the tension and compression zones. Four different reinforcement placement configurations were investigated. An epoxy-based adhesive was utilized for bonding. In accordance with European standards, four-point bending tests were performed on a total of 20 reinforced and 10 unreinforced beams. The reinforced beams achieved significant improvements in mechanical properties relative to the reference elements. For a cross-sectional reinforcement ratio of 4.71%, the maximum mean increases in load-bearing capacity and stiffness were 93% and 94%, respectively. Conversely, the minimum increases for these parameters were 45% and 34% at a reinforcement of 1.57%. The reinforced beams exhibited enhanced ductile behaviour resulting from the plasticisation of the compression zone. However, in many cases, ultimate failure was governed by the fracturing of the LVL in the tension zone. Consequently, the variation in ductility gain between the series was substantial, ranging from a minimum of 8% to a maximum of 37%. In summary, utilizing conventional, widely available, and relatively inexpensive steel reinforcement – as an alternative to composite bars – can significantly enhance the structural characteristics of veneer-based beams.

Circular additive manufacturing of recycled PEKK–regolith composites for sacrificial structures in lunar in-situ resource utilization
abstract: Circular additive manufacturing enabled by in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) offers a promising approach for fabricating sacrificial structures for long-duration lunar missions while minimizing material payload and waste. In this study, recycled poly(ether ketone ketone) (PEKK), recovered from end-of-life sacrificial components, was compounded with 30 wt% lunar regolith simulant (LRS) to produce a recyclable composite filament for material extrusion (MEX) additive manufacturing. The recycled composite was processed by twin-screw extrusion and used to fabricate standardized mechanical specimens, Schwarz-G gyroid lattices, and a functional demonstrator. Thermal analyses showed that recycling and regolith incorporation preserved the thermal stability and crystallization behavior of PEKK, while the reduced cold-crystallization temperature indicated improved annealing efficiency resulting from enhanced thermal transport and heterogeneous nucleation by the ceramic filler. Dynamic mechanical analysis confirmed stable viscoelastic behavior in both amorphous and annealed conditions. Mechanical testing revealed orientation-dependent tensile and flexural properties governed primarily by porosity and interlayer bonding rather than polymer degradation. Compression testing of gyroid lattices demonstrated progressive plastic densification and high energy-absorbing behavior in the amorphous state under quasi-static loading, whereas annealing increased stiffness at the expense of ductility. A NASA-style ratchet wrench fabricated from the recycled PEKK/LRS composite demonstrated material reusability, while regolith incorporation significantly reduced annealing-induced shrinkage and improved dimensional stability. Overall, the results demonstrate the feasibility of closed-loop additive manufacturing of sacrificial components using recycled PEKK reinforced with lunar regolith, supporting circular manufacturing strategies based on ISRU-compatible materials for future lunar exploration.

abstract: The structural application of flax fiber reinforced epoxy composites is constrained by poor fiber–matrix interfacial bonding and high moisture absorption. This study investigates graphene oxide (GO) fiber surface coating to enhance the mechanical performance, thermal stability, and marine durability, demonstrated from laminate to full-scale structural level. GO was deposited onto flax fibers via a scalable coating process at concentrations of 0.75, 1.5, and 2.5 wt.%. The modified fibers were used to fabricate composite laminates and a full-scale marine hatch demonstrator using vacuum infusion moulding. The results revealed significant improvements in flexural strength and interlaminar shear strength, while a reduction in tensile strength was observed, attributed to fiber surface modification during the coating process. Thermal analysis revealed enhanced thermal stability and rigidity at moderate GO loadings. Water resistance improved significantly, with moisture uptake reduced by approximately 25% at the laminate level and by up to 40% in the hatch demonstrator when 1.5 wt.% GO-coated fibers were employed. The findings demonstrate that controlled GO fiber surface modification is an effective approach for durable natural fiber composites in marine environments.

3D-printed hierarchical porous thick electrodes enabling high-energy-density Zn-ion batteries
abstract: Zn-ion batteries are promising energy-storage systems for the post‑Li era. The thick electrode technology enables increased mass loading of active materials, offering significant potential to enhance areal energy density. However, increasing electrode thickness often leads to poor mechanical stability, prolonged diffusion lengths, and sluggish reaction kinetics. Herein, structural engineering is employed to fabricate thick electrodes featuring robust electronic conduction networks and aligned electron/ion transport channels. A novel ink composed of PANI-intercalated V2O5 nanosheets anchored on nitrogen-doped hollow carbon fibers delivers 81% capacity retention with a coulomb efficiency of 99.8% after 4000 cycles at 10 A g−1. Density functional theory calculations reveal that NHCF incorporation promotes Zn-ion (de)intercalation. The thick electrodes with aligned hierarchically porous structures are fabricated via direct ink writing, exhibiting a specific capacity of 327.9 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g−1 with a high-mass-loading of 13.6 mg cm−2. Even at 32.4 mg cm−2 and a thickness of 1050 μm, an areal capacity of 8.98 mAh cm−2 is achieved at 10 mA cm−2. Simulations further demonstrate faster reaction kinetics and higher active-material utilization compared with planar electrodes. This work provides a promising strategy for designing customized high-performance thick electrodes.

title: Multiscale interface-engineered meta-aramid composite papers for robust dielectric and mechanical reliability under harsh environments
Fracture behavior of pultruded GFRP composites under transverse tension at elevated temperatures
abstract: Elevated temperature effects in pultruded glass fiber reinforced polymer (GFRP) composites are typically evaluated through reductions in stiffness and strength; however, the temperature dependence of translaminar fracture toughness remains poorly understood despite its critical role in damage tolerance. This study presents a combined experimental and computational investigation of Mode I-dominated transverse tensile translaminar fracture at service-relevant temperatures up to 80 °C. Wide compact tension (WCT) tests were conducted to quantify crack growth resistance and fracture toughness. The results reveal a pronounced and non-linear temperature sensitivity of fracture toughness, with a sharp reduction between 40°C and 60°C (retention from 97% to 56%), which differs from the comparatively gradual degradation of conventional transverse tensile properties and storage modulus. This disproportionate reduction indicates that fracture energy degradation cannot be inferred from conventional property trends and is governed by temperature-dependent crack-propagation mechanisms, including matrix softening and its reduced ability to dissipate energy and to blunt crack tips. Despite this sensitivity, the previously reported exponential relationship between fracture toughness and transverse tensile strength appears to persist within the investigated temperature range. Finite element (FE) simulations incorporating temperature-dependent properties further demonstrate that accurate structural predictions require explicit representation of temperature-dependent fracture parameters, with the bilinear damage evolution law providing better resistance estimates compared to the linear-exponential law. These findings provide a basis for improved predictive modeling and design of pultruded GFRP structures operating under elevated service temperatures.

Continuous in-situ synchrotron micro-XCT observation of thermoplastic composite laminate consolidation
abstract: The present work deals with the in-situ simultaneous microscopic and macroscopic observation of thermoplastic composites laminate consolidation under hot press conditions. With this aim, first the inCO2TO setup was developed. Then, microscopic observations of porosities evolution by fast micro-XCT were carried out at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. Finally, a 3D image processing methodology enabled to draw several important conclusions. They show that a decompaction phenomenon occurs when the temperature reaches the melting onset point, mainly at ply interfaces by a substantial increase of voids. Pressure has been demonstrated effective to limit this phenomenon and consequently reduce the presence of voids. Different void reduction mechanisms were identified by statistical and morphological analysis within plies and at the interfaces depending on consolidation pressure. A main outcome is the difficulty to eliminate interlaminar voids at low pressure whereas medium-sized intralaminar voids are significantly reduced.

Multiscale modelling of matrix-crack percolation and gas leakage in fibre-reinforced composites at cryogenic temperatures
abstract: A multiscale framework is presented for predicting matrix-crack percolation and gas leakage in fibre-reinforced composites without empirical calibration. By eliminating fitting parameters, the approach provides clear advantages over existing models. A new continuum formulation enriched by a micromechanical damage model is first developed to predict matrix-crack spacing in individual plies, overcoming the dependence of conventional methods on destructive experimental measurements. By explicitly analysing fibres, matrix, and fibre-matrix interfaces, the formulation significantly reduces input requirements to a small set of constituent properties obtainable through standardized testing. The outputs are subsequently upscaled into a laminate-level continuum damage mechanics model to determine matrix-crack spacing as a function of applied strain. This crack-spacing information defines the geometry of a representative unit-cell model used to quantify throat areas at crack intersections. Unlike previous approaches that assume arbitrary delamination lengths, the present framework provides a physically based determination of throat areas. These micro-meso scale predictions are then coupled with an orifice flow model to enable complete leak-rate prediction of macroscale structures without empirical inputs. This novel multiscale framework is shown to accurately reproduce experimental leakage data. Its capability for design and certification of cryogenic fuel storage vessels is demonstrated by quantifying the benefit of increased matrix toughness in enhancing resistance to gas leakage.

Ion-mediated topological optimization of graphene fiber frameworks for high-performance thermal interface materials at ultralow loading
abstract: The escalating heat flux in miniaturized electronics requires high-performance thermal interface materials (TIMs) for efficient thermal management. However, conventional polymer composites suffer from a persistent trade-off between thermal conductivity, filler loading and processability. Herein, we report a novel Ca²⁺-mediated assembly strategy to fabricate topologically optimized graphene fiber frameworks (GFFs) for polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composites. By precisely regulating the fusion degree, this approach transforms discrete fiber networks into interconnected skeletons, establishing continuous through-plane phonon transport channels while minimizing interfacial scattering. Remarkably, the produced GFF/PDMS composite achieves a superior through-plane thermal conductivity of 5.91 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at an ultralow filler loading of only 2.5 wt%, representing a ~30-fold enhancement compared to pure PDMS. More importantly, due to the established vertical conduction pathways and excellent surface conformability, the contact thermal resistance of GFF2/PDMS (55.11 K mm2 W-1) is reduced by one order of magnitude compared to commercial counterparts. Consequently, in real-time chip dissipation tests, the composite delivers exceptional cooling efficiency, yielding a massive temperature reduction of 66.5 °C relative to the pure matrix. This work provides a scalable paradigm for constructing low-loading, high-efficiency thermal management materials via topological structure design.

Meso-structural optimization of patch-based composites for high-value prepreg offcuts reformatting
abstract: Up to 50% of the prepreg acquired by composite part manufacturers is discarded as offcuts due to nesting limitations. Treating those offcuts as waste represents a significant economic loss and a critical sustainability challenge. Since the material remains uncured, however, these offcuts can be reformatted into Patch-Based Materials (PBMs). Engineered meso-structures that control patch position and orientation, such as the Brick-and-Mortar (BaM) architecture, deliver the highest mechanical property retention.This study examines the tensile behavior of engineered PBMs derived from four distinct prepreg systems, evaluating property retention relative to the neat parent materials. Firstly, a theoretical analysis is provided for the influence of key design variables: patch length, parent material properties, i.e. cured ply thickness and interlaminar fracture toughness, and patch spatial arrangement. Experimental results demonstrate that increasing patch length from 5 to 50 mm increases asymptotically both stiffness and strength. Furthermore, utilizing prepregs with reduced thickness and enhanced toughness shifts the primary failure mode from delamination to fiber fracture, achieving the 50% theoretical strength limit in standard BaM architectures. Notably, when fiber-dominated failure is achieved, implementing a modified staggering pattern, called BaM 1/3, further elevates strength retention up to 66%.By elucidating the influence of these critical design parameters, this work provides a framework for maximizing the value of prepreg offcuts and to facilitate the transition toward a circular economy in composite manufacturing.

Revealing statistically robust strain rate effects on mechanical performance of pristine single fiber aramids
abstract: High-performance synthetic fibers, especially aramid fibers, are widely used for body armor applications for their strength, stiffness, and excellent strength-to-weight ratio. Among those, Kevlar and Twaron (hereafter Aramid A and Aramid B, respectively) are extensively used for their superior thermal stability, high modulus, and proven ballistic performance. However, their tensile behavior under high strain rate (HSR) conditions close to ballistic impact remains insufficiently characterized due to experimental challenges in measuring stress and strain at break at the single-fiber level. Previous studies have suggested moderate strain rate sensitivity in aramid-based fibers, but small sample sizes and limited accuracy in failure strain measurement under HSR have constrained the statistical robustness of the findings. In this study, a custom single-fiber tensile Kolsky Bar instrument was configured for HSR tensile testing with accurate specimen alignment, gripping, and pulse quality. A rigid-body digital image correlation (DIC) method was implemented to track relative grip displacements and measure the strain at failure, enabling accurate measurements of failure force, strain, and strain rate at the single-fiber level. Using 62 samples per fiber at HSR and 100 per group under quasi-static (QS) conditions, clear strain-rate-dependent strengthening was observed in both fiber types. Maximum force, failure stress, and failure strain increased by approximately 30 % to 35 % under HSR compared to QS. The large sample size enabled a statistically robust assessment using distributional and non-parametric analyses, showing that Aramid B exhibited more uniform failure distributions than Aramid A. The approach established a practical framework for quantifying single-fiber strain-rate sensitivity.

title: Integrated computational investigation of interfacial bonding and stress mitigation mechanisms in C/C-SiC/410B stainless steel brazed joints
Interlaminar toughening of flax/Elium® composites using asphaltene-derived carbon fibre interleaves
abstract: Natural fibre composites exhibit limited resistance to interlaminar crack growth, particularly under mode II loading, which restricts their applicability in structural components. This study examines a composite interleaving strategy using short asphaltene-derived carbon fibres produced by centrifugal spinning. A wet-laying process adapted from papermaking was used to fabricate 72 gsm interleaf without binders, consolidating fibres into randomly-oriented mats without extensive processing. Similar mats were also produced using commercial PAN-derived carbon fibres to establish a performance benchmark. Flax/Elium® laminates with an interleaf layer in the mid-plane were manufactured by vacuum-assisted resin infusion and tested according to ASTM D5528 (mode I) and ASTM D7905 (mode II). Neither interleaf type significantly changes mode I fracture toughness, despite some mechanistic changes. In contrast, the asphaltene-derived interleaf increases mode II fracture toughness by 40%, and the commercial carbon fibre interleaf increases it by 86%. Scanning electron microscopy confirms that both interleaf types induce crack deflection in the interleaf layer and increase propagation path tortuosity, resulting in higher shear-driven energy dissipation. This study presents a feasible manufacturing route for interleaved composites using wet-laid nonwoven fibre mats and demonstrates that asphaltene-derived carbon fibre interleaves can effectively improve mode II delamination resistance while largely maintaining the mode I fracture toughness in natural fibre thermoplastic composites.

title: Interface-engineered CdS/WO3/NiNb2O6 ternary nanocomposite as a visible-light-active photocatalyst for hydrogen production: Laboratory-scale to large-scale demonstration
Dynamic matrix and interfacial Diels-Alder bonding endows graphene oxide/polyurethane nanocomposites with self-healing, mechanical robustness, and enhanced hydrogen barrier performance
abstract: Hydrogen barrier materials capable of retaining effective barrier performance after mechanical damage are highly desirable for hydrogen storage and transportation applications. Here, we report a functionalized graphene oxide reinforced polyurethane nanocomposite containing Diels-Alder (DA) bonds, denoted as fGO/PU-DA, in which dynamic DA linkages were incorporated into both the polymer matrix and the nanofiller-matrix interface. The 5 wt% fGO/PU-DA nanocomposite achieved a tensile strength of 9.8 MPa, corresponding to a 75% increase over neat PU-DA, while maintaining a favorable balance between strength and ductility. After cut-healing treatment, the nanocomposite recovered nearly all of its tensile strength, whereas its elongation at break and toughness exceeded their original values. The hydrogen permeability coefficient decreased from 2.4 × 10-12 for neat PU-DA to 8.6 × 10-13 cm3·cm·cm-2·s-1·Pa-1 for the 5 wt% fGO/PU-DA nanocomposite, corresponding to a reduction of 64%. Even in the healed state, the permeability remained markedly lower than that of healed PU-DA, indicating a clear barrier advantage after macroscopic damage. Mechanistic analysis indicated that the enhanced barrier performance was diffusion-dominated and originated from interfacial confinement together with reduced cooperative segmental mobility. The material was further validated as a coating on polyamide 6 substrates, where the fGO/PU-DA layer also delivered improved hydrogen barrier performance. These results demonstrate that dynamic bonding in both the matrix and interface provides an effective route to polyurethane nanocomposites integrating self-healing capability, mechanical robustness, and superior hydrogen barrier performance.

title: Predicting inclusion-type internal defects in composites with complex structural shapes from experimental infrared thermography and numerical simulations: A demonstration of a machine learning approach based on graph neural networks
abstract: This study proposes a machine learning-based framework for predicting three-dimensional internal defects in a complex-shaped carbon fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) specimen, using experimentally measured thermoelastic and computational FEA stress distributions. The proposed method employs a graph neural network (GNN), which directly incorporates the FEA mesh. First, high-frequency noise in the thermoelastic two-dimensional stress distribution is removed via Fourier analysis. Then the denoised field is mapped, using partial least squares and Gaussian process regression, into the principal component analysis (PCA) latent space of two-dimensional FEA stress distributions. Next, a multi-layer perceptron projects the latent variables of the two-dimensional stress fields into the latent space of the three-dimensional FEA stress distributions. The resulting latent variables are then reconstructed via PCA to obtain the three-dimensional stress distribution. Finally, the reconstructed three-dimensional stress distribution is input to a GNN trained on FEA datasets to predict three-dimensional internal defects. Conventional nondestructive inspection techniques for CFRP structures, such as X-ray imaging and ultrasonic testing, face safety, cost, and geometric constraints. In contrast, infrared stress measurement offers safer, simpler, and real-time inspection within the field of view. The proposed method estimates internal defect positions from surface stress information and provides a basis for reducing expert-dependent interpretation in future workflows. The present study demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed framework using one complex-shaped CFRP specimen with curved surfaces, such as a prosthetic-leg geometry, under the prescribed defect conditions.

title: Two-phase numerical modeling of interfacial dynamics in overmolding of thermoplastic composite inserts with short fiber-reinforced thermoplastics
abstract: Understanding the interfacial interactions between molten short fiber-reinforced thermoplastics and pre-molded continuous fiber composite inserts during overmolding is essential for optimizing adhesion, stress distribution, and the mechanical performance of the final part. This study introduces a novel and streamlined numerical approach to model the formation of this complex interface during the overmolding process. A two-dimensional, two-phase flow model is developed by solving the Stokes equations in both the low-viscosity short fiber polymer suspension and the highly viscous thermoplastic composite phases. This strategy eliminates the high computational cost typically associated with traditional fluid–solid interaction (FSI) models. A single equation is solved across the entire domain with only varying viscosities in the two phases.To capture fiber–flow coupling effects within each phase, the model employs a modified constitutive equation that incorporates a fourth-order orientation tensor. This tensor represents the influence of fiber orientation on flow behavior and is computed by directly solving the Fokker–Planck equation using the Streamline-Upwind/Petrov–Galerkin (SUPG) finite element method, enabling the dynamic tracking of fiber orientation over time. The model is validated through simulations investigating how variations in fiber concentration and orientation influence the deformation of the composite insert.The results show that this method achieves improved accuracy while significantly reducing computational cost, making it a promising tool for advancing research in fiber-filled polymer processing. Moreover, the approach provides a foundation for more sophisticated simulations of real-world overmolding scenarios involving fiber-reinforced thermoplastics.

A mechanics-informed framework for fiber length selection in discontinuous CFRTP: Integrating impact performance and cascade recycling
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced thermoplastic (CFRTP) architectures span a reinforcement continuity spectrum from continuous unidirectional (UD) laminates through sheet molding compound (SMC) to carded non-woven fabric (NWF), reflecting a cascade pathway from virgin to recycled fiber. This study investigates how reinforcement length, orientation, and localized continuity govern impact performance, processability, and downstream recycling compatibility, focusing on thin-ply SMC with 44 μm tapes. Previous studies established static property saturation near 20 mm, but the length required for dynamic energy absorption remained unclear. Three-point bending impact tests showed that impact strength and specific energy absorption continued to increase from 20 to 30 mm. This condition also matches the input length required for NWF carding, indicating convergence between improved impact performance and downstream processing compatibility. NWF with controlled anisotropic ratios represented the next recycled stage. UD represented the cascade origin and upper performance bound and was locally over-molded onto SMC, increasing energy absorption without added mass when further gains from tape length or anisotropic ratio became impractical, a key consideration in automotive design. Tape length, orientation, and hybridization therefore provided complementary, architecture-dependent contributions to impact response. Because idealized morphology did not accurately predict SMC response, measured tape geometry and orientation were incorporated into multiscale representative volume element (RVE) modeling, reducing prediction error from 10-16% to below 3% and enabling finite element (FE) simulations with deviations below 15%. Integrating performance, manufacturability, and recycling constraints identified a system-specific design window and established a mechanics-informed framework for fiber length selection in discontinuous CFRTP systems.

Experimental and multi-scale simulation study on carbon nano-filler reinforced friction materials for automotive dry clutches
Dual-action anti-mold wood fibers functionalized with Zn-Al layered double hydroxides and stearic acid coatings
abstract: Wood fibers offer promising sustainable alternatives to synthetic options; however, their susceptibility to mold limits their widespread adoption. Here we report a facile strategy to fabricate anti-mold wood fibers via in-situ growth of Zn-Al layered double hydroxides (LDHs) followed by stearic acid (STA) post-coating. Electrostatic interactions drive the adhesion of LDH to wood, while STA provides surface hydrophobicity, as revealed by molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting wood fibers exhibit remarkable anti-mold activity against common fungal species, including Aspergillus , Trichoderma , and Penicillium , showing clear inhibition zones and no fungal growth in accelerated tests. Further analyses reveal that the direct antifungal effect arises from electrostatic absorption, oxidative stress induction, and metal ions release, while the indirect effect is due to hydrophobicity. Our findings demonstrate a scalable and cost-effective approach for functionalizing natural fibers to combat microorganisms, broadening the application scope of cellulose-based materials in construction, packaging, and biocomposites. We anticipate this work to be a starting point for developing wood fiber composites with intrinsic mold resistance for health- and eco-conscious applications.

title: Editorial Board
Laminated CNT–RGO/Al hybrid composite: High-cycle fatigue strength and impact energy absorption
abstract: In this work, a laminated Al-matrix composite (AMC) reinforced by a 3D-interlaced CNT–RGO network (3:1 CNT: RGO, 1.5 wt%) using flake-powder metallurgy, spark plasma sintering, and extrusion was developed. In the process, ∼550 nm sized lamellae and a density of > 98% were achieved. The 3D CNT-RGO hybrid network plays an essential role in enabling superior load transfer, dislocation fixation and crack deflection, resulting in exceptional high-cycle fatigue and notch impact properties measured at room temperature on extruded bars, with CNT/Al, RGO/Al, and unreinforced Al controls processed identically. Axial fatigue (ASTM E466, R = −1, 10 Hz) yielded a fatigue strength of 322 ± 12 MPa at 10 7 cycles for the hybrid material (+51% compared to CNT/Al, +69% compared to RGO/Al, +262% compared to unreinforced Al), with a fatigue efficiency m = 0.65 (compared to 0.55/0.53/0.51), Basquin exponent b ≈ 0.03 (vs. 0.05–0.07), and Weibull shape β ≈ 8–12, indicating slow damage accumulation and high reliability; the lifetime at 70% UTS reached 9 × 10 5 cycles (+800% vs. CNT/Al, +350% vs. RGO/Al, +2150% vs. unreinforced Al). Instrumented mini-charpy impact (ASTM E2248/ISO 14556, KLST geometry, 5 J) resulted in a peak force of 808.7 N, an absorbed energy of 2.332 J, and a normalized toughness of K V , norm = 0.086 J m m − 2 (+115% vs. unreinforced Al) at reduced deflection (3.75 mm vs. 4.33 mm in Al). Fractography showed the largest propagation fraction ( ϕ f ≈ 0.63) and tortuosity (TI ≈ 1.32), of the hybrid with terraced facets, RGO deflection, and CNT bridging/pull-out ( ≤ 1 μm) and bridging-ligament traces of 1–5 μm, in contrast to the smoother paths in the controls. The percolation network provides intrinsic strengthening (load sharing and back-stress hardening in sub-μm lamellae) and extrinsic toughening (crack expansion and wake shielding), by converting more energy into plastic work and maintaining UTS fractions at cycling. These ∼2-5 times improvements position the hybrid material in a rare high-performance range for Al MMCs and provide a scalable path for vibration/impact-loaded lightweight components.

title: 2D bio-inspired reinforcement mesh for toughening composite bonded joints: Effect of orientation and adhesion patterning
abstract: Inspired by the sacrificial bonds and hidden lengths mechanism found on the molecular structure of spider silk, this study investigates a bio-inspired overlapping curl (OC) 2D-mesh fabricated via 3D-printing and integrated into the adhesive layer as a reinforcement architecture. Mode I double cantilever beam tests were conducted to investigate the effects of mesh orientation (0° and 45°) and adhesion patterning on crack propagation and fracture toughening. The results show that the 2D-OC mesh itself effectively activates extensive filament bridging, leading to an apparent energy release rate (ERR) enhancement up to 47 %. In contrast, adhesion patterning partially suppresses bridging. X-ray computed tomography and fracture surface analyses further reveal that reinforcement orientation governs crack front evolution and bridging activation. In particular, the 45°-oriented mesh induces a zig-zag crack front that promotes crack deflection and bifurcation, thereby activating more bridging filaments than the 0°-oriented configuration. Based on these observations, a coupled toughening framework is established, linking the apparent ERR enhancement to the combined effects of adhesion patterning width, reinforcement orientation, bridging activation, and filament material behavior. The findings provide mechanistic insight into crack–reinforcement interactions and offer design guidelines for architected bio-inspired reinforcements in adhesively bonded composite structures.

Torsional damage behaviour of multilayer braided CFRP tubes observed by time-resolved in situ synchrotron X-ray CT
abstract: Multilayer braided composite tubes are widely used in torsion-critical structures, yet their damage behaviour remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate vacuum-infused single-, double- and triple-layer ±45° diamond-braided carbon fibre/epoxy tubes under torsion using in-situ, time-resolved synchrotron X-ray computed tomography. Increasing the number of layers promotes interlayer nesting and modifies the mesoscale architecture, producing a through-thickness variation in fibre volume fraction and a reduction in tow crimp from the inner to the outer layers. Although the effective shear modulus changes only marginally (∼8.2–8.5 GPa), the shear strain at damage initiation increases from ∼0.5% in single-layer tubes to ∼0.75% and ∼1.0% in double- and triple-layer tubes, respectively. Damage in the double- and triple-layer tubes is dominated by interlayer and inter-tow debonding, whereas single-layer tubes show predominantly intra-tow cracking. Microscale fibre buckling/kinking is also delayed in the multilayer tubes, consistent with the through-thickness tow-crimp gradient and additional lateral confinement. The multilayer tubes further exhibit a more stable post-peak response, with no pronounced load drops in the load–displacement curves. Overall, these observations show that changing the number of braided layers substantially alters the mesoscale tow architecture and, in turn, governs the torsional damage response of braided composite tubes.

Reactive diluents applied in composite-processing methods –thermoset composite production strategies, characteristics, and sustainable opportunities
abstract: Several composite manufactures depend substantially on incorporating reactive diluents to optimize the flow behavior of the employed reactive resins, commonly unsaturated polyesters (UPE), vinyl esters (VE), epoxy systems, and several other highly viscous systems that require suitable low-molecular-weight curable molecules to reduce their viscosity. Styrene exemplifies the main low-cost, available, and efficient compound for radically polymerizable systems (UPE, VE), while possessing high volatility, health and environmental risks, and an entirely fossil-based structural character. Methacrylate and vinyl derivatives are introduced in this work as versatile and complex alternatives to styrene for reactive diluting, often absenting volatility and even exhibiting lower hazardous character, but their functional performance is frequently limited. Epoxy systems do not necessarily require rheology modifications like UPEs and VEs; however, the specific functional modification is commonly required for optimal material performance. In particular, pultrusion, as a continuous process, usually employs reactive diluents in the fabricated matrices to control composite fabrication. In addition to the discussion of the specific exploited structural reactive diluents, the primarily affected properties were covered, including viscosity, thermo-mechanical character, mechanical attributes, and interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) specific to fiber-reinforced polymer composites (FRP). The structural character, specific functional groups within the carbon backbone, and the reactive functionality (the number of polymerizable centers) significantly influence the final composite. Eventually, this comprehensive review suggests specific reactive diluents from renewable sources as sustainable alternatives to currently used systems, offering innovation, systems diversification, and potentially safer solutions.

Compliant auxetic cementitious composites for piezoresistive sensing
abstract: Auxetic cementitious cellular composites (ACCCs) exhibit high compressive deformation with recoverable behavior, demonstrating strong potential for self-sensing applications. In this study, compliant piezoresistive ACCCs were engineered to combine auxetic behavior with piezoresistive properties by reinforcing a cementitious matrix with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and carbon fibers. Uniaxial compression tests were conducted to evaluate their piezoresistive responses in damage sensing across distinct deformation stages, while Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Acoustic Emission (AE) techniques were employed to investigate corresponding deformation and damage mechanisms. Cyclic loading tests further assessed the flexible sensing behavior of ACCCs within the recoverable deformation during the auxetic behavior range, with further insights obtained from microscopic analysis and X-ray computed tomography (CT). The piezoresistive sensing behavior of two typical ACCC specimens with different geometries was compared. The results demonstrate that the auxetic behavior promotes high compressive deformation, which can be delineated into four distinct mechanical stages. Each stage corresponds to specific damage mechanisms and exhibits characteristic piezoresistive responses, as reflected by stage-dependent variations in the fractional change in resistance (FCR). This staged behavior effectively extends the sensing range for damage detection. Under cyclic loading, the composites exhibit a reproducible piezoresistive response across an extended self-sensing range, attributable to their substantial recoverable deformation. This behavior highlights their superior strain and stress sensitivity, although residual plastic deformation progressively increases with greater loading amplitude. Given wide availability of cementitious materials, highly deformable ACCCs with piezoresistive strain/stress and damage sensing capabilities offer a cost-effective and sustainable solution for in-situ, real-time structural health monitoring.

abstract: Dimensional stability, often requiring near-zero coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) combined with high tensile modulus, is essential for precision structures in space observatories, interferometric platforms, and advanced manufacturing systems. Fiber-reinforced composites are the current state-of-the-art for achieving near-zero CTE without sacrificing stiffness; however, the coupled design space spanning constituent properties, fiber volume fraction, and laminate architecture is typically explored through multi-objective optimization schemes. While effective for a fixed material system, such approaches provide limited physical insight on viable fiber–matrix combinations. Moreover, deterministic laminate theory assumes that constituent and manufacturing parameters take single nominal values, whereas in practice these quantities vary and can shift the laminate response away from the predicted zero-CTE condition. To address these limitations, we propose a Stochasticity-aware Laminate Design (SaLD) framework. First, a rapid screening method based on the non-dimensional thermoelastic parameter that identifies compatible fiber–matrix combinations by directly relating constituent properties to the fiber volume fraction required for zero-CTE. A stochastic laminate formulation then propagates material and manufacturing variability through sub-ply discretization to predict distributions of modulus and CTE. Global Sobol sensitivity indices quantify parameters governing output spread, while a Jensen-based index captures systematic shifts in the mean response relative to deterministic predictions. The analysis further shows that higher laminate stiffness suppresses CTE variability and that stochastic averaging across sub-ply microdomains significantly reduces laminate-level variability. Guided by these insights, iterative adjustments of design and process parameters reduce variability and realign the response toward zero-CTE, providing a practical pathway for designing dimensionally stable composite laminates.
