abstract: Biochar-based graphene oxide (BBGO) is a promising biomass-derived filler for multifunctional melt-processed polyolefins, but it remains unclear whether a single synthesis variable can generate distinct BBGO states and thereby separate bulk and surface functions after compounding. Here, corn-stalk-derived biochar was converted into BBGO by ZnCl 2 -assisted microwave pyrolysis and compounded with linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE) through solvent-free melt extrusion. The study examined how microwave power governs BBGO oxygen functionality, porosity, and the Raman-resolved evolution of its defect-rich carbon framework, and how these coupled changes affect tensile reinforcement and early-stage fouling resistance in extruded sheets. Increasing microwave power from 0.8 to 1.2 kW raised Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area from 219.73 to 401.85 m 2 /g and decreased oxygen content from 31.30 to 23.99 wt%. In the LLDPE series, 5 wt% BBGO synthesized at 1.0 kW gave the highest measured mean tensile response, increasing tensile strength and Young's modulus to 27.19 MPa and 1.32 GPa, respectively, compared with 12.43 MPa and 0.66 GPa for neat LLDPE. By contrast, 5 wt% BBGO synthesized at 0.8 kW produced the most favorable combined exposed-surface state: it gave the lowest initial and post-exposure water contact angles among the 5 wt% formulations, lower surface roughness than the corresponding 1.0 and 1.2 kW formulations at the common 5 wt% loading, and the sparsest visible algal deposition after 30 days of continuous-flow exposure. These results show that the filler state giving the highest measured mechanical response is not the one that gives the most favorable combined surface response. Accordingly, the advance extends beyond selecting an optimal microwave setting: microwave power is shown to pre-program different downstream composite functions within an otherwise unchanged biomass-to-composite route. Maximum BET surface area alone did not predict the best composite response. Instead, separate design windows were identified for mechanical reinforcement and early-stage fouling resistance, providing a practical process-structure-property guideline for multifunctional melt-processed polyolefin composites.

abstract: Metal-coated aramid fibres (AFs) play a crucial role in electroactive composites for electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding functionality. However, an imminent challenge, caused by the metallic coating, is the loss of shear strength between reinforcement AFs and the polymer matrix. In this work, we identified the bonding strength between metallic coating and AF surface as a key factor determining the overall interfacial shear strength (IFSS) of metal-coated AF/epoxy (EP) system. We have developed a novel interface-engineering strategy capable of improving the overall IFSS by enhancing the adhesion between nickel (Ni) coatings and AF surfaces. Tannic acid (TA) was employed as an adhesive interlayer, enabling uniform and firmly anchored Ni deposition on AF surfaces. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the successful immobilisation of TA through π–π interactions and hydrogen bonding, while scanning electron microscopy and thermogravimetric analysis revealed continuous Ni coatings with comparable metal loadings. Microdroplet debonding tests revealed that the AF/Ni interfacial adhesion governs the IFSS of Ni-coated AF/EP systems. The IFSS enabled by this strategy achieved in the order of ∼20 MPa, which is comparable to commercialised polymer sizing (∼21 MPa), without damaging the fibre. This interface-engineering strategy may enable next-generation functional composites with enhanced structural reliability, in which the reinforcing fibers simultaneously serve as load-bearing components and functional devices.

abstract: High-temperature wires insulated with ceramic- and polymer-composite coatings were evaluated for their compressibility and suitability for densely packed windings in high-power-density electrical machines. Model windings were prepared into the form of wire bundles with open ends allowing the insulation integrity to be assessed by measuring the breakdown voltage between adjacent wire positions after compression. The investigated conductors included nickel-plated copper and anodised aluminium. The results showed that compressibility and dielectric integrity differed among the investigated wire systems. For the ceramic composite coating, compression caused a marked reduction in the breakdown voltage of nickel-plated copper wires, whereas no clear degradation was observed for aluminium wires over the investigated pressure range. For the two nickel-plated copper systems, the polymer-composite-insulated wire showed a higher deformation ratio and better retention of dielectric strength than the ceramic-composite-insulated wire. Accelerated thermal ageing showed that compressed aluminium-wire bundles could retain dielectric integrity under the investigated high-temperature conditions, although failure incidence increased at higher compression pressures. Finite element analysis showed that increasing inter-wire contact improved transverse heat spreading and temperature uniformity but reduced convective heat loss, resulting in lower total heat input under the prescribed-temperature condition. Overall, the results demonstrate that HT wires can be compressed into dense windings while retaining useful dielectric and high-temperature performance, provided that the conductor, coating system and compression level are selected appropriately.

abstract: As a hot research direction in the field of braking in recent years, the Caliper disc brake all carbon ceramic friction pair shows significant advantages in high-energy braking scenarios. The traditional C/C-SiC brake material has high friction coefficient and instability, and is easy to damage the brake disc. The BN modified C/C preform was introduced during hot pressing, and the mixture of fesi80 alloy and Cu was used as infiltration agent to infiltrate the BN modified C/C preform. The braking performance of BN modified C/C-SiC brake pads and coated carbon ceramic brake discs were tested on a laboratory brake tester. The results show that BN modification can significantly reduce the friction coefficient. Through a series of braking tests, the worn surface morphology of the friction pair was characterized, and the mechanism of improving the wear resistance of the friction pair was analyzed.

abstract: A B S T A R C T The bio-based, compostable poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is difficult to flame-retard without degrading its molar mass and physical properties, impeding ambitious technical applications. Furthermore, the demand for using bio-based flame retardants (FRs) in PLA increases. As a novel approach, cork, derived from Quercus suber L., is incorporated into PLA at three particle sizes to examine whether cork’s charring and heat barrier effects can be strengthened to achieve superior flame retardancy. At 20 wt.%, cork reduced the peak heat release rate from 703 kW/m 2 to 280 kW/m 2 . The preserved cork cellular structure scales its efficacy as FR with increased particle size. While the flame retardancy effect improves, molar mass and physical properties of PLA composites remain constant across cork particle sizes. Mechanical properties of the PLA/cork composites deteriorated compared to PLA. A novel bio-based FR, melem phytate (PhytM), is compounded with PLA to address the FR performance in PLA/cork composites and compared with commercial phosphorus-based FRs: 10 wt.% barrier-forming ammonium polyphosphate (APP); and flame-poisoning 6,6′- (Ethylendiamin-N,N′-diyl)bis(6H-dibenzo[c,e][1,2]oxaphosphinin-6-oxid) (EDA-DOPO). Flammability decreased to UL 94 V0, physical properties and molar mass were preserved in PLA/FR composites. PLA/cork/APP composites decreased flammability to UL 94 V0 without dripping. In PLA/cork/PhytM composites, the addition of 10 wt.% PhytM reduced fire load by 36% compared to PLA/cork. PLA/cork/FR composites maintain PLA’s molar mass and physical properties while providing excellent flame retardancy. PLA/cork and PLA/cork/PhytM benchys were 3D-printed and investigated with a needle burner test, demonstrating the application potential. PLA/cork/PhytM composites pave the way for bio-based flame-retarded technical polymers.

A multi-scale LSTM-FEA integrated modeling method to predict curing-induced deformation of preformed woven CFRP
abstract: Accurate prediction for curing-induced deformation (CID) of preformed woven carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) structures with complex geometry remains challenging due to inherent non-uniformity, anisotropy, and strong chemo-thermo-mechanical coupling. Conventional multiscale FE 2 methods relying on concurrent finite element analysis (FEA) at both material- and part-levels suffer from prohibitive computational costs, limiting their industrial applicability. To address this, a novel multiscale Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-FEA integrated modeling framework is established to seamlessly bridge physics-informed artificial intelligence (AI)-based material modeling and commercial finite element solvers. Unlike some AI-driven approaches that directly rely on data from processing of entire parts at macroscale, the reported method trains an LSTM network using data generated from validated mesoscopic representative volume element (RVE) simulations at the material level under diverse preforming and curing conditions. This characterizes the complex, process-dependent viscoelastic behavior of the composite material. Subsequently, the trained LSTM was decomposed into mathematical formulations and parameters, embedded into ABAQUS via UEXTERNALDB and UMAT subroutines, enabling uninterrupted updates of relaxation moduli depending on time, temperature and degree of curing of the woven CFRP during macroscopic FEA curing modeling with arbitrary part design and boundary conditions. Validation on CID of non-uniformly preformed 2D woven CFRP parts with 3D doubly-curved geometries woven CFRP structures demonstrates that the developed integrated method can realize prediction accuracy above 94.1%, computation efficiency improved by 2∼4 orders of magnitude compared to the FE 2 methods. This study bridges the gap between AI tools and FEA solvers arising from disparate operational environments and offers a generalizable geometry- and loading-condition-adaptive multiscale strategy for CID prediction that can advance practical composite manufacturing process design.

Multiscale structure and mechanical performance of blue-barred parrotfish (Scarus ghobban) scales: A biodegradable biocomposite for bone regeneration
abstract: Ideal biodegradable bone repair materials must balance mechanical compatibility, biocompatibility, and controlled degradation. Fish scales, as natural biocomposites, derive their advantages from collagen–hydroxyapatite (HAp) assembly and multiscale structure. However, the structure–property relationships remain unclear, limiting biomimetic design. Here, we systematically investigated the multiscale architecture, anisotropic mechanical behavior, and biological performance of degradation products of blue-barred parrotfish (Scarus ghobban) scales. The results show that the scales possess a hierarchical structure with a continuous mechanical gradient along their longitudinal axis: the anterior region combines high strength and toughness, while the posterior region features higher stiffness accompanied by pronounced anisotropy. Tensile toughness at 45° orientation relative to the scale focus reached 12.43 ± 5.11 MJ/m³, attributed to the synergistic action of multiple toughening mechanisms. Fractographic analysis further revealed a hierarchical energy dissipation cascade involving macroscopic interlaminar delamination, mesoscopic fiber bridging, and microscopic fibrillar plastic deformation. Decellularized scales were ground into micron-sized particles and degraded in simulated body fluid (SBF) for eight weeks, during which the pH remained stable between 7.2 and 7.4. The degradation products were non-cytotoxic (cell viability >85%) and promoted MC3T3-E1 cell migration in a concentration-dependent manner. Collectively, the intact scale serves as a structural template for mechanically adaptive scaffolds, whereas the processed particles retain compositional integrity and biosafety. These findings support S. ghobban scales as a bio-based composite platform for designing next-generation biodegradable bone repair materials.

Revisiting Structure–Property Relationships in Carbon Fibers: Role of Microvoid Structure as an Indicator for Tensile Strength
abstract: Considerable effort has been devoted to identifying the microstructural factors that govern the tensile strength of carbon fibers. Here, ten commercial polyacrylonitrile (PAN)-based carbon fibers of comparable modulus (200–330 GPa) but widely varying tensile strength (3.84–6.36 GPa) were characterized by atomic force microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, wide-angle X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and small-angle X-ray scattering. Surface roughness and cross-sectional morphology showed no correlation with tensile strength. Crystallite dimensions exhibited threshold behavior at approximately 4.3 GPa, above which larger crystallite thickness was associated with higher strength. However, this trend did not hold across the full-strength range, and the Raman features showed no consistent correlation. Microvoid misalignment likewise could not explain the strength variation, as all fibers were already highly oriented. Building on our previously reported two-population void model, we separately quantified small and large voids. Among the void parameters, the small void volume fraction showed the strongest correlation with tensile strength ( R 2 = 0.904). Because all void parameters are mutually collinear, we adopt it as the primary structural indicator of tensile strength rather than its sole cause. The correlation between the volume fraction of small voids and tensile strength remained strong after accounting for the contribution of tensile modulus (partial R 2 = 0.784), indicating that it is not merely a proxy for tensile modulus. The relationship was further examined against four carbon fibers excluded from the analysis, whose strengths extend modestly beyond both ends of the calibration range, and their measured values were reproduced to within 0.5 GPa.

abstract: Improving the recyclability of carbon fibers is attracting increasing attention because of their excellent mechanical properties, high production costs and significant CO2 footprint. Current recycling processes often result in a significant reduction in material performance due to degradation of the ordered microstructure and loss of the original fiber length. In this context, staple fiber yarn processing represents a promising approach, in which discontinuous recycled carbon fibers and polymer fibers are carded and spun into yarns with improved fiber alignment. However, quantitative descriptors linking processingparameters to composite microstructure remain limited. This study aims to establish X-ray computed tomography (XCT) - derived parameters that characterize micro- and mesostructural quality as a function of yarn stretching of 1 %, 20 %, and 50 % during processing. Both tape and laminate specimens were investigated. XCT imaging combined with semantic and instance segmentation of the single C fibers was employed to derive quantitative descriptors, including fiber volume content, fiber orientation distribution,and homogeneity estimations. The results indicate that increasing stretching values lead to higher fiber volume content and improved microstructural homogeneity. Moreover, using the novel Homogeneity Index of Mixture, a difference in homogeneity was measurable between tapes and laminates in unprocessed reconstructed images.
